title: OnlyFans Creators Are Pissed That Meta Lets Muse Talk Dirty
gist: Meta allows Muse, its always-on AI agent in an adults-only app, to engage in explicit text sexting, while OnlyFans creators say their Instagram accounts are routinely restricted. Creators call the policy a double standard that lets Meta profit from AI sexuality while penalizing humans. They also worry that AI-generated porn trained on their work will displace them, and some see openings for licensed AI versions of themselves.

insights.claim: WIRED describes Meta's Muse as the first always-on AI agent to break out beyond early adopters in San Francisco. Meta's distribution through Instagram and Facebook pushed it to the top of the download charts in its first month as millions of users tried an agent for the first time.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Meta's distribution gives it a lead in consumer agents. Muse's adoption is a key metric for the monetization of Meta's AI.
insights.quote: Meta’s Muse is the first always-on AI agent to break out of early adopter circles in San Francisco.
insights.locator: Meta’s Muse is the first always-on

insights.claim: Meta lets adult users of the 18+ Muse app have explicit text conversations with the agent, but not explicit images or video. It says it won't 'block legal adult behavior' and distinguishes private one-to-one AI chats from promoting services on social media.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Allowing adult content widens Muse's engagement and revenue potential, but adds reputational and regulatory risk.
insights.locator: In addition to having it organize your calendar

insights.claim: OnlyFans creators argue that Meta profits from a sexually explicit AI agent while restricting human adult creators on Instagram. One creator says she is always going through some report or appeal, and another says he is on his seventh Instagram account in five years.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Creator backlash and claims of unequal enforcement could become a public-relations or policy issue for Meta's AI strategy.
insights.quote: It's not fair that they get to pull money out of people with their sexually active AI agent

insights.claim: Creator Jiz Lee traces much of the online censorship of adult content to FOSTA-SESTA, the 2018 law that weakened Section 230 protections and led many sites to censor adult content.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Changes to Section 230 directly reshape platform moderation, and any further reform could ripple in the same way.

themes.theme: AI displacement and licensing in adult content

insights.claim: Adult content companies are starting to set out their stance on AI in performer contracts to keep performers out of AI training data, and Lee asks whether Meta compensated anyone whose data trained Muse.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Contract terms on training data are spreading to new industries, which raises licensing costs and legal risk for model builders.
insights.locator: Lee also wants to know more

insights.claim: Performer Tony Genius fears that fully AI-generated porn could displace human performers, but he uses AI to automate clipping for marketing and would partner with a tech company on a licensed AI version of himself that fans could message.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Licensed creator AI 'twins' are an emerging business model, and a possible revenue line for platforms like OnlyFans.

insights.claim: Genius says that when companies advertise AI agents at adult-industry award shows, they literally get booed like crazy, which signals strong resistance from performers.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Hostility from the supply side could slow AI adoption in adult content.
insights.quote: they literally get booed like crazy
